Question: Regarding the theory of gradual evolution, how can populations of partially evolved individuals survive their "death sentence" of being handicapped? Isn't evolution the "survival of the fittest"? The partially evolved animal is easy prey, right?
Old_Answer: Wrong. You see, the whole “partially evolved” idea is wrong. At every point, you have an animal which is a slight improvement on what came before. A well-known example is the eye. You start out with a light-sensitive patch on the skin. This way, the animal can know whether it is in the open (potentially dangerous; something might eat it) or hidden beneath something (safer; it’s harder to find). Two patches is better: you can start to “see” which direction light is coming from, and in which direction it is darker. If the patches are in dimples on the skin, the direction sensing gets much better. If they are in a deep recess, it gets even better and you can even get something like an image of the surroundings, with light and shade. A transparent membrane protects your proto-eyes… and this goes on, until you have fully functioning eyes. Every stage is an improvement. There is no such thing as “partially evolved” – all the proto-eyes are useful, and good enough for the animals’ purposes. And we know this because every time the eye gets improved, there’s a part of the population that stays behind, and they are still around – hiding under rocks, in the case of the light-sensitive patch. It’s good enough if all you want to do is to hide from the light. Those two things – gradual improvement and “good enough” – is what is missing from your description. Every step along the way has to improve on what was already there. But your description actually shows why there are still apes – another thing that mystify people with only the sketchiest knowledge about evolution. If apes tried to evolve into humans – or rather, something “human-like” – now, when we are already around, they’d be out-competed in no time at all. They’d be rather bad at being apes, and rather bad at being humans, and they wouldn’t have a “place” of their own in the ecology to occupy. They’d have to do something different – maybe become carnivorous, or living in water, or something else that humans didn’t do. “Omnivorous, savannah-dwelling tool-wielder” is already taken.
Answer_with_writing_sample: The notion that partially evolved individuals are at a disadvantage is a common misconception about evolution. First off, evolution isn’t a linear path toward perfection; it’s a complex process driven by environmental pressures and genetic variation. A partially evolved trait can still offer advantages in certain contexts. For example, consider a species of bird that develops a slightly longer beak. This bird might not be the best at feeding on all types of food, but if its environment changes and it finds itself in a habitat where longer beaks are advantageous for accessing a new food source, then those "handicapped" individuals can thrive. Moreover, evolution operates on populations, not individuals. If a trait is beneficial enough to improve reproductive success, even if it seems like a handicap in other contexts, it can still persist in the gene pool. The concept of "survival of the fittest" is often misinterpreted; it doesn’t mean the strongest survive, but rather those best suited to their environment. Additionally, many traits can have trade-offs. A partially evolved trait might make an individual more vulnerable to predators but could also provide other benefits, such as better camouflage or improved mating displays. In essence, evolution is about adaptability, and what may seem like a disadvantage in one scenario can become an asset in another. So, while partially evolved individuals might face challenges, they can also find niches where their traits are advantageous, allowing them to survive and reproduce.

Question: Of the sci-fi concepts such as faster than light travel, teleportation, and false gravity on space craft (without it spinning), or other, which is the least likely/furthest away?
Old_Answer: That depends on the exact flavour of each of those things. As far as we know, FTL travel throught a “wormhole” is not forbidden by the laws of physics. There might still be an unknown law forbidding it, and it seems a wormhole can’t be stable for long enough to send an object through it, but FTL communication would still be on the cards, as per current knowledge. (Also, we wouldn’t have the faintest clue how to create one, much less manipulate it.) And then we have hypotheticals like the Alcubierre drive, which requires a form of matter we have good reasons to believe doesn’t exist, but no solid evidence against. Teleportation in the shape of the Star Trek “transporter” isn’t as insane as it sounds. What they do is to take you apart atom by atom, scan the exact quantum state of each atom, and then – depending on SF franchise – either send the atoms one by one to be re-assembled at the destination, or just send the information and assemble locally available atoms into an exact copy, indistinguishable even on the atomic level. Absolutely insanely complex, to the point of probably never being possible in practice, but not actually forbidden by the fundamental laws of physics. Whether the copy is actually the same person, though, is a matter for philosophers. (I would tend to say “no”, although I can’t quite articulate why… except by saying you’re never stuffing me inside one of those things.) Artificial gravity is so far off the table that you hardly ever even read about it in SF novels. It only exists in TV and movies, and even so, only as a handwave explanation for why the actors aren’t floating around the room. There is absolutely nothing that would lead us to suspect gravity can be manipulated that way.

So, unless we discover some groundbreaking new physics that allows for warp drives or wormholes, we’re stuck with the cosmic speed limit. Teleportation, on the other hand, while still a stretch, has seen some experimental success at the quantum level, albeit with particles rather than people. It’s a long way from being practical, but at least it doesn’t outright defy the laws of physics. As for artificial gravity without spinning, we’re already exploring various methods, like linear acceleration or magnetic fields, to simulate gravity in spacecraft. While none of these are perfect solutions yet, they’re much more plausible than bending the fabric of spacetime. So, in summary, while all these concepts are fascinating and fuel for imagination, faster-than-light travel is the one that remains firmly in the realm of fantasy, while the others at least have a foot in the door of scientific inquiry.

Question: Where will the gravity of the Earth be zero?
Old_Answer: There is only one: at the center of the Earth. There, the Earth pulls at you equally in all directions, and the net force is zero. Of course, the center of the Earth is filled with metal at immense temperatures and pressure… but there is no gravity (net; there is gravity all around but it cancels out).
Answer_with_writing_sample: The gravity of the Earth will be zero at a point known as the Lagrange Point, specifically L1, which is located between the Earth and the Moon. At this point, the gravitational forces of the Earth and the Moon balance each other out, creating a sort of gravitational "sweet spot." However, it's important to clarify that this doesn't mean gravity is absent; rather, it's a point where the gravitational pull from the Earth is countered by the Moon's pull. So, if you were to find yourself at L1, you wouldn’t float away into the void, but you would experience a unique gravitational equilibrium. Additionally, if we consider the concept of free fall, astronauts aboard the International Space Station (ISS) experience what feels like zero gravity, but that's due to their continuous free fall towards Earth while moving forward at high speed. They are essentially in a state of perpetual free fall, creating the sensation of weightlessness. So, while there are places where the effects of gravity can be minimized or counteracted, true zero gravity in the context of Earth’s influence is more about balance than absence. It’s a fascinating interplay of celestial mechanics that illustrates how gravity isn’t just a simple force but a complex interaction that can vary dramatically depending on your location in the universe.
